name: The Teardown Tradition
scope: What teardowns teach: cost-down archaeology, how professionals read a board, the EEVblog tradition

claims.claim_text: An unidentifiable part in a torn-down product - a chip-on-board epoxy blob over bare silicon, or a device carrying a house label - can still be characterised without ever naming it, by intercepting the serial traffic between it and the parts around it and then spoofing that traffic to exercise the function it controls.
claims.quote_verbatim: Sometimes you have the black blob with just a piece of silicon underneath, or it's got a weird label. So, basically, you know, if you want to go and reverse engineer that, you could intercept the serial stream. You could try and spoof the serial stream.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Older instruments are commonly built around parts carrying a manufacturer's internal number rather than a catalogue number, so no datasheet exists to be found; in a Tektronix TDS 220 teardown the custom National Semiconductor part yielded at best a block diagram, and the practical ceiling on such investigation is identifying the standard part the custom device was derived from and working from that.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, it's got some custom part number. It's manufactured by National Semiconductor. I think something exists out there, maybe a block diagram for it or something, but you know, it's like, no. Yeah. The best you're going to get is like, this is based off this part. And then you go and find that part and try and see if you can, you know, shoehorn that in there.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Space Bound, Again - Xtreme Xtraplanetary Xenonosocomiophobia

claims.claim_text: Enclosures closed by heat welding or ultrasonic welding make a teardown one-way: the case cannot be reassembled afterwards, which is why densely integrated consumer devices are often left intact rather than opened.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm tempted to tear it apart, but I, I don't think it'll go back together, so. Right, it's probably got a heat welded case and an ultrasonic welded case and all that sort of jazz, yeah.

claims.claim_text: How much there is to say about a board is set by how many separately partitioned functional blocks the design contains: a high-performance radio front end presented twenty-five distinct blocks to walk through, where an oscilloscope teardown offers nothing like that number.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, there were 25 separate blocks that I went through there. I mean, you know, your average... If you tear down an oscilloscope, there's not 25 different blocks to talk about.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Taking finished gear apart and studying how it was designed and constructed is treated as part of an engineer's ordinary learning process rather than an optional curiosity.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, look, if you're not taking gear apart and at least, you know, doing teardowns and looking at how things are designed and constructed, you're missing out on a huge.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A teardown can expose an omitted process step rather than a bad part: one product was found to have no conformal coating at all, and an owner hardened his own unit by applying conformal coating inside it after seeing the bare boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: For some reason, they don't conformal coat it, and so he was... He hardened his design.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A modern flagship phone is built as a screen layer and a single layer of everything else, and within that layer the battery accounts for roughly sixty percent of the volume - the dominant constraint on what else can be fitted.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like, so first off, I always think it's really interesting the amount of battery space, right? So, basically, this whole thing is single layer, right? The whole phone is basically, it's like a screen layer and then it's got a layer of stuff. And then within that layer of stuff, what, 60% of it is battery?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Of the non-battery volume in a flagship phone, roughly thirty percent is circuit board and roughly ten percent is camera modules carried on flexible boards, with rigid-flex construction used where a single part must be partly board and partly flex.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, then of the remaining percentage-wise, it's probably 30% circuit boards and then probably 10% is like camera modules that are like flex boards. Flex, what is that called? Like mixed media or whatever. So, it's like rigid flex where it's like some parts are circuit boards, some parts are flex.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Regulatory compliance filings are a public source of pre-release internal photographs, since a radio product must be submitted for certification before it can be sold; the filings routinely include device photographs and internal views that amount to a teardown published ahead of launch.
claims.quote_verbatim: So lots of, lots of creepiness there, but, but the FCC, uh, site is really cool to look at. I mean, you can find a lot of, um, devices and product pictures and teardowns and stuff like that. That's how a lot of the Apple fanboys get their pre-information is because you have to submit it to the FCC for compliance before you put it on sale.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Parts harvested from torn-down equipment accumulate into a specific storage problem: items too large or too low in value to sell individually but plainly useful to someone, which practitioners clear in bulk at swap meets rather than piece by piece.
claims.quote_verbatim: Probably the biggest problem is the stuff which is too big or too low value to eBay, but you just can't bear to throw away. Exactly. That's the really hard stuff. Obviously, there's a lot of stuff I pull out of teardown gear that is potentially useful to somebody, but it's just a pain in the ass to me.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A cost-driven teardown of an instrument proceeds chip by chip across the board with the cost of each part added up, and the exercise is informative precisely because a precision instrument is obliged to use precision parts to meet its published specifications.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like I'm about to go through the teardown, go through every chip on the board and add up the cost. Right. Because this is a precision instrument. Yeah. Right. It, it needs precision parts to meet these specifications.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Visual inspection alone will not settle what a board contains, because parts and structures hidden under packages or inside the stack-up require X-ray to see.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think you need a x-ray machine though too, because you might be surprised.

claims.claim_text: A teardown teaches how an existing design was solved, but the subtle design considerations only become visible when the same thing is implemented; that implementation stage routinely takes two to ten times longer than first estimated.
claims.quote_verbatim: Um, cause I, I just find it fascinating how much you can learn from tearing down an existing design. And then, uh, and then you really learn it when you try to implement it yourself. That's when you really learn that, you know, a lot of the, the very, uh, subtle, you know, design considerations and, you know, the stuff that it takes you two to 10 times longer than you originally anticipated.
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: Large end-of-life office equipment such as a colour laser printer is torn down as a parts-harvesting exercise as much as an inspection one, the object being to establish which mechanisms and assemblies inside are worth salvaging.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, so what I was going to do is actually put a big mat down on the floor and I was going to tear it apart. That was going to be today's video, tear it apart and see what parts you can salvage from one of these big, like sort of corporate laser color laser printers.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Published teardown cost estimates account only for the major chips and give no reliable figure for what a product costs to make; a real cost requires assembly, transportation, warehousing and the rest of the vertically integrated manufacturing chain to be added.
claims.quote_verbatim: No, well, you'll get those on like iFixits when they do a teardown. And I think they kind of might do a cost estimate of, you know, like the basic chips used in there at least, you know, but no, if you want the real cost, you have to factor in all the assembly and transportation and other warehousing, you know, all the costs associated with actually manufacturing, vertically integrated manufacturing and entire phone.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Opening a phone shows how much of it is custom in the mechanical domain rather than the electrical one: custom plastics and tooling are comparatively accessible, whereas taking a chip custom means going the whole way through the semiconductor process, which is why bespoke mechanics appear long before bespoke silicon does.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think the other thing that's interesting about this is like, like seeing in the mechanical realm too, so much of it is custom. Right. And, you know, there's obviously, you know, chip, phone manufacturers are moving into their own chip space, right? Apple's doing their own chips and the other Samsung does their own chips. And like, that's not out of the realm of possibility, but it's not like they're just, you know, turning around and spinning up a, you know, a stamping plant that, or, you know, they cut a new die to do a new chip. They have to actually go all the way through the process. And in the mechanical realm, it's like, there is a lot of custom stuff, especially in the plastics and, you know, like, because there's just more tools for doing that sort of thing.

claims.claim_text: Someone opening products every week reports that nothing fundamental about how electronics is made has changed: boards are still laid out on fibreglass laminate, components are still soldered to them, catalogue parts are still bought through distributors, and only the size and capability of the parts have moved.
claims.quote_verbatim: We're still buying catalogue parts at the, you know, we've still got the distributors that we're dealing with. We've still got this. We've still got, well, nothing's inherently changed. Just the components have got its smaller, you know, greater capability, blah, blah, blah. But ultimately, we're still making products in the electronics industry exactly the same way we always have.
claims.episode_title: Compare and Contrast Tech Entitlement - Worldly Working Wonks

claims.claim_text: Withholding a schematic protects very little when the part numbers on the board are legible, because anyone can reverse-engineer the schematic from the physical product in about a day - which is the argument for publishing the schematic while keeping the firmware source closed.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think that like, cause there's no, you know, like, because anyone can reverse engineer the schematic in a day. Because otherwise you would just do your own teardown of your own product. Yeah, no, it's like, it's stupid. Like it's not going to then, you know, the numbers aren't going to be rubbed off the chips, you know? So I think it's a given the schematic will be, you know, available for the thing.
claims.episode_title: Don't Turn It On, Don't Take It Apart

claims.claim_text: Teardown has been used as formal university teaching material rather than only as informal practice: Kent Lundberg ran a class built on tearing down products such as guitar pedals.
claims.quote_verbatim: He was tearing down guitar pedals, stuff like that. Was it at MIT or maybe at Olin? I forget. But he was doing some of that stuff.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Reverse-engineering a radio product does not require extracting its firmware: tapping the bus between the microcontroller and the radio chip reveals the protocol, after which a substitute microcontroller can be connected to the same radio chip and made to drive it.
claims.quote_verbatim: And, uh, I just reverse engineer the radio protocol. So instead of trying to dump the firmware in this case, I tapped the communications between the microcontroller and the radio chip. And just looked at that and then connected my own microcontroller to the radio chip and was able to do it that way.
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: A teardown can be continued past the board to the die: chemical decapsulation of a package yields die photographs, giving a level of detail below the board-level inspection that most teardowns stop at.
claims.quote_verbatim: Speaking of chemicals that'll take things apart, Electron update did a teardown of ESP32. I thought that was pretty good too. It was nice kind of going down through the various levels. I had not seen any die shots of that.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Potted assemblies defeat teardown entirely, since the compound cannot be removed without destroying what it encases, so potting is an effective barrier to inspection as well as to moisture.
claims.quote_verbatim: Anyway, I would love to do a teardown, but sorry. It's like, I think it's like potted or something.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Systematically tearing down consumer products to see how they work is a route into identifying which silicon platforms serve ultra-low-cost designs, and pairs with keeping public written notes because the knowledge is otherwise held only in the practitioner's head.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I think I was looking at CH32 V003 since a couple of months, and then during August timeframe in 2023, I got some time free for a couple of weeks, and then I thought, okay, this is an interesting platform for ultra low-cost, you know, products, and I was already doing teardowns, you know, to figure out how the whole consumer electronic works, and, you know, that really matches my interest, and, you know, I started learning, and then I realized, okay, I'm learning, and I'm keeping the whole learning in my head.
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: The specific test applied when judging cost-cutting from a teardown is derated headroom rather than brand: capacitors rated 200 volts on a 300-volt bus are a legitimate fault to call out, whereas 600-volt parts in sufficient number on the same bus are sound engineering even when the brand is unfamiliar.
claims.quote_verbatim: So if they look like they're in good condition and it's marked on the side that they're, you know, the proper... Like, if they're, like... They're 105. Say they have a 300-volt bus and they're rated at 200 volts, I would call that out, right? But, like, if it says they're, you know, 600-volt rated caps and it's a 300-volt bus and it looks like there's enough of them.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Marketing claims about component quality are checkable by teardown and do not always survive it: one inverter shipped with a glossy brochure devoting a full page to its use of named premium components including Nippon Chemi-Con capacitors and Panasonic relays, and none of those parts were present in the unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it came with a brochure, you know, a big glossy brochure about how DI is the best thing ever. And they've got a whole page in there devoted to how they use the best quality components. And they put the logos there. They've got Nippon Chemicon caps. They've got Panasonic relays. They've got, you know, this brand semiconductor in there and all that sort of thing. So I did the teardown video and none of them are in there. None of them are in there.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A consumer tracking tag that appears functionally trivial is not trivial inside: the board is comparatively complex and the device carries two separate printed circuit boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: And so I was looking at his stuff and some of the other, you know, teardowns and things like it. And it's pretty, I mean, it's a complex little board for sure. It's definitely more complex. I didn't think there was much in it. I thought it was just like. There's two PCBs in there.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Clap on, clap off, lights flicker

claims.claim_text: Smartphone internals are dominated by flexible circuits terminated in very low-profile board-to-board connectors that snap together, which is the interconnect style a teardown of any modern handset will encounter.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, in a phone, like a smartphone, if you open it up, there's going to be flex cables or flex circuits with these very, very low profile connectors that snap into each other.
claims.speaker: Davide Andrea
claims.episode_title: All the Connectors with Davide Andrea

claims.claim_text: A retail price far below what the visible content should cost is itself a reason to open a product: an e-book reader sold boxed at retail for thirty Australian dollars carried a seven-inch colour TFT screen.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, I like e-book readers, but, you know, it's a heap of shit, but I wanted to, the reason I bought it is because it's 30 bucks. 30 bucks. Australian. Right? 30 bucks. That's crazy. Yeah, it comes in, that's retail, right, at the local Dick Smith store, right, in a nice package, you know, a nice big plastic form package. I'm going to do a video of it, you know, I'll do a tear down, and it's got a seven-inch color TFT screen on it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The premise of reading a board is that nothing inside is inexplicable: every product opened is the output of a team of engineers working for a period of years, so each choice visible on the board had a reason behind it that can in principle be recovered.
claims.quote_verbatim: I mean, you do teardowns. I rip stuff open, you know, like, it's not like crazy, undescribable stuff, right? Everything can be explained. A team of engineers spent two years building it, you know?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Teardown has been run as the spine of an electrical engineering prototyping course, on the reasoning that one would not design a bridge without first studying how bridges are built.
claims.quote_verbatim: I mean, it's like you wouldn't build a bridge without, you know, studying how bridges are made. So it's basically a teardown course. It's a teardown course.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Part-number lookup is the bottleneck in a teardown at the bench: without a datasheet-capable screen beside the work, the practitioner shuttles to a desk machine for each unknown part and loses the several specifications just memorised on the way back.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I'm back and forth to the desktop machine during the teardown just trying to find, you know, these part numbers. And then often by the time I get back to the bench, oh, I've forgotten those specs because I'll try and remember them, right? And I'll go, oh, yeah, that chip has this bandwidth and it has this, you know, these features and this feature. And I've got to remember those five things to go back to the… Yeah, exactly.
claims.episode_title: eReaders, datasheets & board assembly - Yearly Yeasty Yapping

claims.claim_text: A teardown that contains no surprises is still a valid result: confirming that a product holds exactly what its function implies, and no more, is an outcome rather than a failed investigation.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh yeah, that was good. It's not that surprising. There's not much in it. Duh. Like, you know, it's had exactly in it what I expected to be in it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: Agilent's low-end oscilloscopes were formerly rebadged Rigol instruments, and the company subsequently brought design and manufacture of that range back in house.
claims.quote_verbatim: But the big news is that Agilent are now designing and manufacturing these low-end scopes in-house. So, everyone knows that they used to rebadge the Rigol ones, right? And I don't know if that was a success or failure for them. I guess it was a failure. They've gone back in-house, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: What separates a low-cost oscilloscope built by a large instrument maker from one built by a smaller competitor is custom ASIC development: the smaller firms lack the research budget to develop such chips, and once the development cost has been paid the chip itself costs only a few dollars per unit, which is what enables the low selling price.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the technology is so advanced in this scope that these other small pissant companies like Rigol, even though they're the third biggest scope, or fourth biggest in the world or something like that in terms of technology, I think, they can't do. They don't have the technology in the R&D to do the kind of ASIC chips which go into these new scopes. So, really. And that's what it's enabled the low cost. Right. Yeah. It pulls all that stuff in. Because once you've put in the R&D funding to do that chip, you can churn out the chip like it's nothing, you know? Right. It costs, you know, I don't know, a few bucks to churn out this advanced chip which makes the most advanced, one of the most advanced low-end scopes in the world.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: Commercial teardown-analysis services exist as an industry in their own right, iSuppli among them, selling structured breakdowns of competitors' products.
claims.quote_verbatim: Maybe there's a service like, I know there's the tear down service, like a, I supply is one of them, but I don't know if they do that for cars.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Freescale, Hackerspaces, Printable Electronics - Publish Popular Parts Please!

claims.claim_text: Teardown is a route to reviving obsolete capital equipment rather than only to inspecting it: a Phantom V4 high-speed camera dating from the early 2000s was torn down and returned to working order.
claims.quote_verbatim: The whole thing came about when I got a Phantom V4, which is an old high speed camera from the early 2000s, did a teardown, was able to get it working.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: One thing a teardown reveals directly is vendor concentration: an Agilent U1272A handheld meter was found to use a large number of Maxim parts, showing which supplier had won the analogue content of the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: Anyway, it's interesting to mention Maxim, because in my recent teardown of the new Agilent U1272A meter, I noted, if you have a look at the video... Oh, I should go watch that video right now, Dave. Absolutely. I need the views. Yeah, they use a ton of Maxim parts in there.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BASIC, Chip companies & Robots - Pernicious Projects, Puppies in Peril

claims.claim_text: Publishing a debunking teardown carries legal exposure: a forum member who bought a fuel-saver device, reverse-engineered its schematic and showed it could not work was threatened with a lawsuit by the company selling it, with demands for damages and removal of the material, though nothing came of the threat.
claims.quote_verbatim: Um, actually bought one of these things and did a tear down of it and actually reversed engineered the schematic and everything. It's fantastic. Yep. And he debunked the whole thing saying, you know, this thing's a crock and it can't work. And, um, then he got threatened, um, with a lawsuit by the company that sells it. Cause it's a big company. They sponsor NASCARs and you know, they're making a lot of money out of this fuel saver device.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Opening a clipped consumer enclosure is done incrementally with a knife, popping one clip at a time on the assumption that the process is still reversible, and the commitment to a full teardown accumulates clip by clip rather than being decided at the start.
claims.quote_verbatim: But, you know, I sort of got my knife out and I popped off one clip. And I thought, oh, okay. And you just get the temptation. Close enough. You pop off the next clip. Oh, you know, look, I can always go back if I get too scared. And I start popping off more.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Board count alone tells a reader where a product sits: finding more than one circuit board inside a toy is itself the signal that the design was pushed far beyond the norms of its category.
claims.quote_verbatim: Actually, so Fictive did a teardown of the Ultimate Lightning McQueen teardown. So it's... Yeah, it's... I mean, kind of like the exploded view of everything that's in there too. Even just like having more than one circuit board in a toy.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A promotional toy sold at three hundred dollars carried six motors, a miniature LCD behind the character's eyes and Bluetooth control throughout, which is the content that puts such a product outside the toy category on cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: But it's got like six... So it's got like six motors on it. It's got like a... Like the cars... Where the cars' eyes are usually in the screen. It actually has like a mini LCD and stuff like that. And it's just... And it's all Bluetooth controlled.

claims.claim_text: An instrument bought for 8.70 US dollars with free shipping met its published specifications and looked acceptable inside, but carried no manufacturer name at all: the name and model number had been physically abraded off the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: And anyway, so I was like, it was $8.70 US, right? Free shipping. So I ordered one of these things and I've got one in my hand now. It just turned up. And sure enough, it works. It seems to meet its specs. The teardown inside looks okay. It is completely no name, right? And it looks like they've actually scrubbed off physically on the product. They've scrubbed off the name and the model number.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The connector-versus-hardwire decision is one of the oldest in product design and is legible from a teardown: soldered-in cables save connector cost but force desoldering before boards can be separated for service or inspection, and a product that mixes proper board-to-board interconnect with hardwired links in the same assembly indicates the decision was not made consistently.
claims.quote_verbatim: Do you go for an all connector solution? Do you hardwiring? Like when I'm doing a tear down of a product, I go, oh geez, they've hardwired in these, you know, look, Sony, the bastards. They've like hardwired in these cables, right? They're soldering them in. And how do I get these boards apart? And I've got to unsolder the bloody things just to take the boards out so I can like poke around at them and stuff. It's like, you know, but no, somebody deemed that that was, you know, cost saving or some other, you know, thing that they wanted to do and they weren't going to go, you know, or they will mix them. Like you, you tear down a product and you go, well, this is half board, nice board to board interconnect and half hardwired sold. And it's like, what the hell?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Electrostatic discharge discipline during a teardown is commonly reduced to an antistatic mat with a wrist strap used only when a board is judged to warrant it, on the reasoning that ordinary careful handling of a finished product is itself a fair test of how robust that product is.
claims.quote_verbatim: And quite frankly, I'd be very concerned if a product I took apart, especially when I was actually still using an ESD mat, so I'm actually taking more precautions than most people would. Yeah. And yes, I do occasionally wear my strap if I deem it to be important. But if I'm doing a tear down of a board, I typically don't wear it out of sheer laziness. And I think, well, it's not a bad test anyway.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Texas Instruments, OPA & Chevy Volt - Nerdy Neuroelectronic Neurosis

claims.claim_text: Third-party teardown cost analysis put the bill of materials of a 199 US dollar Kindle at around 203 dollars, implying the hardware was sold below cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: $199 US dollars and everyone, apparently some expert company's done a tear down, and added up the bill of materials and stuff like that. And they say, oh, this make, it's $203 to make it or something. And they're making a loss.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Such bill-of-materials estimates systematically understate a large buyer's position, because a manufacturer forecasting sales of eight million units within four months commits to and pays for that volume of parts up front, at prices a per-unit teardown estimate cannot see.
claims.quote_verbatim: I, I think they're underestimating Amazon's buying power. Cause they estimate they'll sell 8 million of these things in the, as you say, like the first four months or something. Four months.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
